issues.subcategory: Mislabeled standard error as standard deviation
issues.description: Throughout the results, the authors report 'SD' for parameter estimates from the cross-lagged model. These should be 'SE' (standard error), not 'SD' (standard deviation). Standard deviations of parameter estimates are not a meaningful quantity in SEM; what Mplus reports alongside unstandardized path coefficients are standard errors. This mislabeling recurs for every reported parameter.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.03, -.01])

issues.subcategory: RMSEA confidence interval inconsistent with point estimate
issues.description: The reported RMSEA point estimate is .03, but the 90% CI is [.025, .026]. This confidence interval does not contain the point estimate, which is mathematically impossible. Additionally, the CI width of .001 is implausibly narrow even for a very large sample. This suggests a transcription error or misreporting of the fit indices.

issues.subcategory: Implausibly large chi-square difference value
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the cross-lagged paths between SDO and RWA yields Δχ²(1) = 15,389.13, which is extraordinarily large for a single degree of freedom test comparing two path coefficients. This value is orders of magnitude larger than the other chi-square difference tests reported (50.98 and 39.97) and seems implausible, suggesting a computational or reporting error.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (χ2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: Poor model fit dismissed inadequately
issues.description: The CFI of .86 falls below both the liberal (.90) and conservative (.95) thresholds commonly recommended for acceptable model fit. The authors dismiss this by attributing it to 'model complexity,' but CFI is actually a relative fit index that already accounts for model complexity through comparison to a baseline model. A CFI this low raises concerns about model misspecification. The SRMR of .07 is also borderline. Accepting a poorly fitting model undermines confidence in the parameter estimates.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: Traditional CLPM without random-intercept decomposition
issues.description: The authors use a traditional autoregressive cross-lagged panel model (CLPM), which conflates between-person and within-person effects. Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman (2015) demonstrated that CLPM estimates can be misleading because stable between-person differences drive the cross-lagged associations, making them appear as within-person causal effects. A random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) would separate trait-level (between-person) associations from within-person change processes, providing much stronger evidence for the causal claims the authors wish to make. This limitation is not discussed.
issues.quote: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.subcategory: Narrow operationalization of environmentalism
issues.description: Environmentalism is measured with only two items assessing willingness to sacrifice for the environment. This is an extremely narrow operationalization of 'environmentalism,' which is a multidimensional construct encompassing beliefs, concerns, attitudes, and various behavioral intentions. The discussion frequently generalizes from 'willingness to sacrifice' to 'environmental attitudes,' 'environmentalism,' and 'environmental exploitation,' which far exceeds what the 2-item measure captures. The abstract similarly states conclusions about 'the motivation to exploit the environment' despite only measuring sacrifice willingness.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate causal claims from CLPM
issues.description: The authors make explicit causal claims ('causal pathway,' 'causal effect,' 'infer causal associations') based on cross-lagged panel models. Even with longitudinal data and cross-lagged designs, causation cannot be established because (1) the CLPM does not separate within- from between-person effects, (2) unmeasured time-varying confounders are not controlled, (3) the measurement intervals are annual and may not match the actual causal lag, and (4) no experimental manipulation was employed. The causal language is unjustified throughout.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.subcategory: No reporting of attrition or retention rates
issues.description: For a five-year longitudinal study, there is no information about how many participants completed measures at each time point, what the retention rates were, or whether attrition was systematic (e.g., differential dropout related to SDO, RWA, or environmentalism levels). The total N of 22,974 is mentioned but it is unclear whether this represents those who completed at least one wave or all five waves. Systematic attrition could bias cross-lagged estimates, particularly if individuals high in SDO or low in environmentalism are more likely to drop out.
issues.quote: Of the 22,974 participants included in this study, the average age was 43 years at Time 1

issues.subcategory: FIML incorrectly described as imputation
issues.description: Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) is described as an imputation method, but FIML does not impute missing data. Instead, it estimates parameters using all available data by maximizing the likelihood function for each case based on the variables that are observed. This mischaracterization suggests a misunderstanding of the missing data method employed, which could affect confidence in the appropriateness of its application.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: Missing RWA item at Time 2 not addressed
issues.description: The authors note that one RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but do not explain how this was handled in the latent variable model where factor loadings are constrained to equality across time points. If the item is simply missing at one wave, this creates an asymmetry in the measurement model that could affect the invariance constraints and latent variable estimates at Time 2. The implications for measurement invariance and model estimation should be discussed.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the 'normal way' things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: Measurement invariance assumed but not tested
issues.description: The authors constrain factor loadings, intercepts, and residual variances to equality across time points (implying strict measurement invariance), but do not report any tests of whether these invariance constraints hold. Measurement invariance should be tested sequentially (configural, metric, scalar, strict) with model comparison tests before imposing constraints. If invariance does not hold, the constrained model could yield biased estimates of the cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the factor loadings of our latent variables to equality so that, for each factor, the individual items that make up the factor were set to be equal across time points.

issues.subcategory: Stationarity assumption imposed without justification or testing
issues.description: The authors constrain all cross-lagged parameters to be time-invariant (stationarity) because they are 'more interested in the overall and comparative effects.' However, the stationarity assumption is substantive and testable—the relationship between ideology and environmentalism could plausibly change over a five-year period (e.g., due to political events or natural disasters). The constrained model should have been compared against an unconstrained model to determine whether stationarity is tenable, or at minimum a theoretical justification for stationarity should be provided.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: No covariates or demographic controls
issues.description: The model does not include any demographic covariates (e.g., age, gender, education, income, political affiliation) that could confound the relationships between SDO, RWA, and environmentalism. For instance, gender is associated with both SDO (men score higher) and environmentalism (women tend to score higher), and education is related to all three constructs. Without controlling for these variables, the cross-lagged paths may reflect spurious associations driven by stable demographic differences.
issues.quote: The model thus included three latent variables across five measurement points, where each variable within a time point was set to predict each variable in the subsequent time point.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming generalizability despite demographic imbalances
issues.description: The authors claim results are 'highly generalisable' based on a 'nationally representative sample.' However, the sample is 86% Pākehā (New Zealand European) and 62% female. New Zealand's actual demographic composition includes approximately 17% Māori and 15% Asian populations, suggesting the sample substantially overrepresents Pākehā. The gender imbalance also limits representativeness. Furthermore, generalizability to other national contexts is not discussed despite known cross-cultural variation in SDO-RWA relationships.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory claims about SDO-RWA relationship expectations
issues.description: In the introduction, the authors predict 'reciprocal cross-time effects' between SDO and RWA, citing Duckitt's model and the polarized New Zealand political context. However, the results show a unidirectional effect (RWA→SDO only). In the discussion, the authors then cite Duckitt et al. (2002) to explain the non-significant SDO→RWA path as expected in authoritarian-conservative contexts, directly contradicting their stated prediction. The post-hoc explanation reverses the theoretical rationale used to generate the prediction.
issues.quote: Therefore, on the association between SDO and RWA over time, we expect reciprocal cross-time effects... This contradicted our initial expectations, however it is consistent with Duckitt et al. [23]

issues.subcategory: Conflation of environmentalism with climate change throughout discussion
issues.description: The discussion extensively discusses climate change (psychological distance, IPCC findings, climate impacts on disadvantaged groups, climate change communications) despite the measure capturing general willingness to sacrifice for the environment, not climate change attitudes specifically. The measure does not reference climate change at all. The implications drawn about climate change denial, climate communications, and climate justice go well beyond what the operationalized construct can support.
issues.quote: Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications.

issues.subcategory: No descriptive statistics for Time 2-5
issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics are presented. For a five-wave longitudinal study, descriptive statistics (means, SDs, reliabilities) at each time point are important for evaluating potential mean-level changes, measurement quality consistency across waves, and potential cohort or practice effects. The sample sizes at each wave are also not reported.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration disclosed
issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for this study, despite the use of a large existing dataset (NZAVS) that offers substantial researcher degrees of freedom in variable selection, model specification, constraint choices, and significance thresholds. The choice of a p < .01 threshold, the specific stationarity constraints, and the decision to use traditional CLPM rather than alternatives (e.g., RI-CLPM, latent growth models) all represent analytic decisions that could have been pre-registered.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a conservative p-value threshold of p < .01 to indicate significance of findings

issues.subcategory: Standardized estimates not presented in main text
issues.description: Only unstandardized parameters are presented in the main text, with standardized estimates relegated to supplementary materials. Since the unstandardized estimates are not directly comparable across different constructs (SDO, RWA, and environmentalism have different scales and variances), standardized estimates would be necessary to meaningfully compare effect sizes. The claim that SDO is a 'stronger' predictor than RWA ideally requires comparison on a common metric.
issues.quote: We present unstandardized parameters, which are invariant over time due to the constraints placed on the model. The standardized estimates, which do vary across time points, are included in the Supplementary Materials

issues.subcategory: Confidence interval for willingness-to-SDO path is ambiguous
issues.description: The confidence interval for the lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on SDO is reported as [-.04, -.03], but the point estimate is B = -.04. This means the lower bound of the CI equals the point estimate, which is unusual and likely reflects rounding issues that obscure the actual precision of the estimate. The same issue applies to the willingness→RWA path where B = -.01 and CI = [-.01, -.003].

issues.subcategory: Overinterpretation of cross-lagged effects as motivational processes
issues.description: The authors interpret cross-lagged regression coefficients as reflecting specific motivational processes (e.g., 'the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance'). Cross-lagged paths represent statistical prediction of rank-order change, not motivational processes. The leap from a predictive association to a claim about motivation requires additional evidence (e.g., mediation analyses testing specific mechanisms).
issues.quote: The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.

issues.subcategory: Low reliability of abbreviated scales
issues.description: The SDO (α = .69) and RWA (α = .70) scales have reliabilities below the conventional .70-.80 threshold for adequate internal consistency. While the authors acknowledge this is expected for abbreviated scales, low reliability attenuates observed relationships and could differentially affect the cross-lagged paths for SDO versus RWA. Latent variable modeling partially addresses this, but the small number of indicators (6 items each, 2 for environmentalism) limits the ability to adequately model measurement error, especially with only 2 indicators for the environmentalism construct.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures

issues.subcategory: Two-indicator latent variable for environmentalism
issues.description: The environmentalism latent variable is based on only two indicators. A two-indicator latent variable is just-identified at the measurement level, meaning measurement error cannot be fully separated from the construct. This makes the latent variable estimates fragile and highly dependent on the specific items chosen. Combined with the narrow content coverage, this undermines confidence in the environmentalism construct in the model.
issues.quote: "Are you willing to change your daily routine in order to protect the environment?" and "Are you willing to make sacrifices to your standard of living (e.g., accept higher prices, drive less, conserve energy) in order to protect the environment?"

issues.subcategory: Third variable confounds not addressed empirically
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that third variables could explain the bidirectional relationships but only suggest this as future research rather than testing available confounds. The NZAVS dataset likely includes political orientation, religiosity, income, education, and personality measures that could serve as confounders or mediators. The failure to control for even basic demographic confounds weakens the causal inference substantially.
issues.quote: a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable

issues.subcategory: No effect size interpretation or practical significance
issues.description: The cross-lagged path from RWA to environmentalism (B = -.02) is statistically significant but extremely small. With N > 22,000, trivially small effects can reach significance even at p < .01. The authors do not discuss the practical significance of the effects, nor provide standardized estimates in the main text that would help readers evaluate whether these effects are meaningful in magnitude.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of sampling
issues.description: The abstract describes the sample as a 'national probability sample,' while the discussion section calls it 'nationally representative.' The methods section does not provide sufficient detail about the sampling procedure to evaluate either claim. Given the demographic imbalances (86% Pākehā, 62% female), the sample may be a probability sample with differential non-response rather than a representative sample, and these are distinct concepts.
issues.quote: a national probability sample over five years... Our research uses a nationally representative sample
